rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the full elution window while limiting late-peak penalties. The retention and resolution pattern will identify critical pairs and guide narrower-window and slope tests.

Change only gradient duration to determine whether the crowded early peaks respond to a shallower slope. This also tests whether the later borderline pair gains resolution before optimizing the elution window.

Test temperature selectivity against injection 1 while keeping the gradient unchanged. Higher temperature may separate the crowded early cluster and should keep the final peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

Retain the favorable high-temperature selectivity and use a shallower gradient to improve the sole unresolved pair. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, leaving room to gain resolution without a time penalty.

The remaining close pair did not improve with a shallower gradient, so test a higher starting organic fraction to change its selectivity. Keep 60 C, which substantially improved the early cluster, and monitor retention of the first peak.

Increase the starting organic fraction one more step, following the improvement in the critical pair from R 1.14 to 1.32. This may reach full resolution while further shortening retention; check that the early peaks remain adequately separated.
Injection 6 reached the maximum CRF, so now test a shorter gradient for a faster fully resolved method. Reduce tG by one grid step while holding the successful solvent window and temperature fixed.

Narrow the solvent window to make the 8-minute gradient slightly shallower, aiming to restore both marginal pairs above R 1.5. The endpoint remains well above the last peak’s estimated elution composition, so all compounds should still elute during the gradient.

Test whether raising the starting organic fraction can shorten the fully resolved method from injection 8. This may improve the current limiting pair, but the earlier cluster must be checked for compression.

Return to the fastest fully resolved solvent program and lower temperature one step to probe selectivity between the two critical early pairs. This tests whether a better resolution balance could support further gradient shortening.

Restore 60 C and test a 6-minute gradient with a narrower window, giving a slope between the resolved injection 8 and marginal injection 7. The final organic fraction remains above the estimated last-peak elution composition, while the critical pairs should be close to the full-resolution threshold.

Injection 11’s rounded CRF masks a pair just below full resolution; lower phi1 one step to make the gradient slightly shallower. This should restore R above 1.5 while retaining the shorter gradient duration and keeping the last peak near six minutes.

Test whether a shallower gradient can recover the early pair that became limiting at phi0 0.20 while preserving the improved separation of its neighbor. This explores an alternative fully resolved window with potentially more balanced resolution margins.

The high-temperature branch has reached maximum CRF but resists further shortening. Test the opposite temperature limit for an alternative elution order that might separate the critical cluster under a faster gradient, retaining injection 8 as the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Return to the favorable 60 C selectivity and test a shallower gradient for greater resolution margin while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes. Maximum CRF is already achieved, so this explores a less borderline alternative to the fastest fully resolved method.

Test one endpoint step below the fastest fully resolved method to gain a little resolution margin without the long retention of injection 15. This should preserve maximum CRF with a last peak around 6.4 minutes.

Slightly reduce the slope relative to injection 13 to strengthen its limiting early pair while retaining the better separation of the neighboring pair. This tests a more balanced maximum-CRF alternative, with the last peak expected comfortably before 10 minutes.

Test the remaining endpoint step between the fully resolved injection 8 and the faster but marginal injection 7. This directly checks whether retention can be shortened below 6.04 minutes while preserving full resolution.

Preserve injection 8’s successful gradient slope but end the ramp earlier to test a shorter programmed gradient. The last compounds will elute during the hold, so check whether they remain resolved and finish within 10 minutes.

Raise the endpoint relative to injection 19 to reduce its late hold-phase retention, while extending the ramp enough to protect the critical early pairs. This tests a compact gradient with more resolution margin than injection 8 and an expected last peak below 7 minutes.

Test a modestly shallower gradient than injection 20 to increase the limiting pair’s resolution margin while keeping the final peak well below 10 minutes. Injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method; this run targets a less borderline maximum-CRF alternative.

Slightly steepen injection 13’s successful gradient and shorten its programmed duration to test the speed limit of the phi0 0.20 branch. The early limiting pair should remain near R 1.5, while the final hold should still allow complete elution before 10 minutes.

Refine the established maximum-CRF region between injections 16 and 21, targeting a last peak near 6.7 minutes with minimum resolution around 1.57. This offers more separation margin than the fastest fully resolved method without a time penalty.

Test a slightly steeper slope than injection 22 with a higher endpoint to eliminate its late hold-phase delay. This probes whether the phi0 0.20 branch can remain fully resolved at shorter retention, while injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Use the final injection to test a nearby method expected to retain maximum CRF with more resolution margin than injection 8 and complete elution around 7 minutes. Injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method, with all ten peaks eluting by 6.04 minutes.
